Diagonal Representation of Algebraic Power Series:
A Glimpse Behind the Scenes

This work is based on the author’s master’s thesis (U. of Vienna, 2020), supervised by H. Hauser.
Sergey Yurkevich ††thanks: Supported by the Austrian Science Fund (FWF): P-31338.
Abstract

There are many viewpoints on algebraic power series, ranging from the abstract ring-theoretic notion of Henselization to the very explicit perspective as diagonals of certain rational functions. To be more explicit on the latter, Denef and Lipshitz proved in 1987 that any algebraic power series in nn variables can be written as a diagonal of a rational power series in one variable more. Their proof uses a lot of involved theory and machinery which remains hidden to the reader in the original article. In the present work we shall take a glimpse on these tools by motivating while defining them and reproving most of their interesting parts. Moreover, in the last section we provide a new significant improvement on the Artin-Mazur lemma, proving the existence of a 2-dimensional code of algebraic power series.

1 Introduction

1.1 Basic Notions and Motivation

In all this text, KK will denote a field of characteristic zero, even though most presented results are known to work even for excellent local integral domains. By default, ℕ,ℚ,ℝ\mathbb{N},\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{R} and ℂ\mathbb{C} are sets (equipped with the appropriate algebraic structure) of natural numbers (including 00), rationals, reals and complex numbers respectively. A ring is always commutative with 11 and a ring homomorphism is always unital. By R∗R^{*} we denote the set of units of a ring RR, and R^\widehat{R} stands for the algebraic completion of a local ring with respect to its maximal ideal. If not indicated otherwise, x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) is a vector of nn variables and x′=(x1,…,xn−1)x^{\prime}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1}). In contrast, tt is always one variable and when we write x​txt, we mean (x1​t,…,xn​t)(x_{1}t,\dots,x_{n}t). Given an nn-dimensional index α∈ℕn\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{n} we write |α||\alpha| for α1+⋯+αn\alpha_{1}+\cdots+\alpha_{n} and xαx^{\alpha} for x1α1⋯xnαnx_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{\alpha_{n}}.

Definition.

A formal power series h⁡(x)∈K⁡[[x]]h(x)\in K[\![x]\!] is called algebraic if there exists a non-zero polynomial P⁡(x,t)∈K⁡[x,t]P(x,t)\in K[x,t] such that P⁡(x,h⁡(x))=0P(x,h(x))=0. Such a polynomial with minimal degree in tt is called a minimal polynomial of h⁡(x)h(x). The set of algebraic power series is denoted by K​⟨x⟩K\langle x\rangle. A power series which is not algebraic is called transcendental.

Consider (x)⊆K⁡[x](x)\subseteq K[x], the maximal ideal inside K⁡[x]K[x] generated by the elements x1,…,xnx_{1},\dots,x_{n}. Then, algebraically speaking, K​⟨x⟩K\langle x\rangle is the algebraic closure of the localization of K⁡[x]K[x] with respect to this ideal, K​[x](x)K[x]_{(x)}, inside K⁡[[x]]K[\![x]\!]. Hence the ring of algebraic power series is a subring of formal power series. Moreover it is easy to see that K​⟨x⟩∗=K⁡⟨x⟩∩K​[[x]]∗K\langle x\rangle^{*}=K\langle x\rangle\cap K[\![x]\!]^{*}. Here are several examples in one variable, x=x1x=x_{1}.

  1. Example 1:

    Any polynomial p⁡(x)∈K⁡[x]p(x)\in K[x] is an algebraic power series since we may chose P⁡(x,t)≔t−p⁡(x)P(x,t)\coloneqq t-p(x).

  2. Example 2:

    The power series given by

    (1+x)r=∑k≥0(rk)​xk,(1+x)^{r}=\sum_{k\geq 0}\binom{r}{k}x^{k},

    for some rational number r∈ℚr\in\mathbb{Q} is algebraic11 1 The function (1+x)r(1+x)^{r} exists for any r∈ℚr\in\mathbb{Q}, because the characteristic of KK is assumed to be zero.. This holds true, because when r=p/qr=p/q for non-zero integers p,qp,q, we may choose P⁡(x,t)=tq−(1+x)pP(x,t)=t^{q}-(1+x)^{p} if p,q>0p,q>0 and P⁡(x,t)=tq​(1+x)−p−1P(x,t)=t^{q}(1+x)^{-p}-1 if pp happens to be negative. We obtain again that P⁡(x,(1+x)r)=0P(x,(1+x)^{r})=0.

  3. Example 3:

    Consider the exponential power series:

    exp⁡(x)=∑k≥0xkk!.\exp(x)=\sum_{k\geq 0}\frac{x^{k}}{k!}.

    We claim that it is transcendental: assume it was algebraic, then after dividing the minimal polynomial by the coefficient of the leading term in tt, we would find a Q⁡(x,t)=q0​(x)+⋯+qm−1​(x)​tm−1+tm∈K⁡(x)​[t]Q(x,t)=q_{0}(x)+\cdots+q_{m-1}(x)t^{m-1}+t^{m}\in K(x)[t] with Q⁡(x,exp⁡(x))=0Q(x,\exp(x))=0. Now, taking the derivative of Q⁡(x,exp⁡(x))=0Q(x,\exp(x))=0 with respect to xx and using exp′⁡(x)=exp⁡(x)\exp^{\prime}(x)=\exp(x), it follows that

    q0′​(x)+⋯+(qm−1′​(x)+(m−1)​qm−1​(x))​exp⁡(x)m−1+m​exp⁡(x)m=0.q_{0}^{\prime}(x)+\dots+(q_{m-1}^{\prime}(x)+(m-1)q_{m-1}(x))\exp(x)^{m-1}+m\exp(x)^{m}=0.

    Subtracting this from m​Q​(x,exp⁡(x))=0mQ(x,\exp(x))=0 and using the simple fact that no rational function q⁡(x)q(x) can satisfy q⁡(x)=c​q′​(x)q(x)=cq^{\prime}(x) for c∈K∗c\in K^{*}, we can find a non-zero polynomial of lower degree than mm also annihilating exp⁡(x)\exp(x). This is a contradiction with the minimality of mm.

  4. Example 4:

    The function f⁡(x)=xf(x)=\sqrt{x} is not an algebraic power series, because it is not a formal power series.

  5. Example 5:

    Set f⁡(x)=x+1f(x)=\sqrt{x+1} and g⁡(x)=x+13g(x)=\sqrt[3]{x+1}; we already saw in Example 22 that both f,g∈K​⟨x⟩f,g\in K\langle x\rangle. To see that f⁡(x)+g⁡(x)=x+1+x+13f(x)+g(x)=\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt[3]{x+1} is algebraic as well, just consider the polynomial

    P⁡(x,t)=t6−3​(x+1)​t4−2​(x+1)​t3+3​(x+1)2​t2−6​(x+1)2​t−x​(x+1)2\displaystyle P(x,t)={t}^{6}-3\left(x+1\right){t}^{4}-2\left(x+1\right){t}^{3}+3\left(x+1\right)^{2}{t}^{2}-6\left(x+1\right)^{2}t-x\left(x+1\right)^{2}

    and verify that it indeed satisfies P⁡(x,f⁡(x)+g⁡(x))=0P(x,f(x)+g(x))=0. Finding such a P⁡(x,t)P(x,t) is not straightforward and may require some work.

Algebraic power series appear in many mathematical areas, such as combinatorics, algebraic geometry and number theory. In order to motivate their deep ring-theoretic study in the next sections, we first introduce a very explicit viewpoint.

  1. Example 1:

    Let x=x1x=x_{1} be one variable and f⁡(x,t)=1/(1−x−t)f(x,t)=1/(1-x-t). Then we obtain

  3. Example 3:

    Consider the well-known power series

    f⁡(t)=∑n≥0∑k=0n(nk)2​(n+kk)2​tn∈ℤ⁡[[t]]⊆ℂ⁡[[t]].f(t)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^{2}\binom{n+k}{k}^{2}t^{n}\in\mathbb{Z}[\![t]\!]\subseteq\mathbb{C}[\![t]\!].

    This series appears in Apéry’s proof of the irrationality of ζ⁡(3)\zeta(3). It is known to be transcendental and to satisfy a Picard-Fuchs differential equation, see [ABD19, AB13]. A lengthy but simple computation shows that f⁡(t)f(t) is the small diagonal of the rational power series

    11−x1⋅1(1−x2)​(1−x3)​(1−x4)​(1−x5)−x1​x2​x3∈ℤ⁡[[x1,x2,x3,x4,x5]].\frac{1}{1-x_{1}}\cdot\frac{1}{(1-x_{2})(1-x_{3})(1-x_{4})(1-x_{5})-x_{1}x_{2}x_{3}}\in\mathbb{Z}[\![x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4},x_{5}]\!].

    In [Str14] a diagonal representation with four variables is shown:

    f⁡(t)=Δ⁡(1(1−x1−x2)​(1−x3−x4)−x1​x2​x3​x4).f(t)=\Delta\left(\frac{1}{(1-x_{1}-x_{2})(1-x_{3}-x_{4})-x_{1}x_{2}x_{3}x_{4}}\right).

    Is is not known whether a similar rational expression using only 3 variables exists; in fact no power series is known for which 4 is provably the least number such that it is possible to write it as a small diagonal of some rational power series in that many variables [BLS17].

There are many theorems in the literature connecting algebraic power series and diagonals of rational functions. For example, Pólya observed already in 1922 that the diagonal of any rational power series in two variables is necessarily algebraic [Pó22]. Furstenberg’s trick from 1967 implies that if f∈K⁡[[x]]f\in K[\![x]\!] is algebraic and x=x1x=x_{1} one variable, then there exists a rational power series R⁡(x,t)R(x,t) with 𝒟⁡(R⁡(x,t))=f⁡(x)\mathcal{D}(R(x,t))=f(x) [Fur67]. In the same paper, he proved that a small diagonal of any rational power series with coefficients in a field of positive characteristic is algebraic. In 1984 Deligne improved on the second result: the small diagonal of any algebraic power series over a field of positive characteristic is algebraic [Del84]. Note that for fields of characteristic 00 neither Deligne’s nor Furstenberg’s statements hold (cf. Example 3 above). Some elementary proofs of Deligne-Furstenberg’s theorem have been found later by Harase [Har88], as well as by Sharif and Woodcock [SW88]. More recent and quantitative progress on this theorem is done by Adamczewski and Bell in [AB13]. Denef and Lipshitz gave a simpler proof already in 1987 and generalized the first theorem of Furstenberg to several variables [DL87]. This generalization stated below uses very abstract theory about the ring K​⟨x⟩K\langle x\rangle and we will present its proof in the last section using the discussed theorems of previous sections. A recent algorithmic confrontation to the viewpoint of algebraic power series as diagonals of rational functions is explained in [BDS17]. Finally, the reader can find Christol’s survey about diagonals of rational functions in [Chr15].

Theorem 1.1 (Denef & Lipshitz).

Let f⁡(x)∈K​⟨x⟩f(x)\in K\langle x\rangle be an algebraic power series in nn variables over a field KK of characteristic zero.22 2 In the original paper [DL87] the statement is more general, allowing for excellent local integral domains instead of only fields of characteristic 0, but the ideas of the proof are the same in the special case we consider. Then there exists a rational power series in n+1n+1 variables R⁡(x,t)∈K⁡(x,t)∩K⁡[[x,t]]R(x,t)\in K(x,t)\cap K[\![x,t]\!] such that f⁡(x)=𝒟⁡(R⁡(x,t))f(x)=\mathcal{D}(R(x,t)).33 3 For completeness we mention that Denef and Lipshitz also proved another similar theorem in their paper. Using a slightly different notion of diagonal, they showed that an algebraic power series in nn variables is the diagonal of a rational function in 2​n2n variables, see [DL87, Theorem 6.2 (ii)].

While the statement of this theorem is completely elementary, its proof uses quite involved techniques of commutative algebra and algebraic geometry. The goal of this text is not only to motivate and explain them to a non-expert reader, but also to provide intuition for the main steps of the original proof. After the prefatory discussion about the ring of algebraic power series in Section 1, we advance to Section 2 which is devoted to the notion of Henselization and its connection to K​⟨x⟩K\langle x\rangle. In Section 3 we introduce étale ring maps and use this tool to prove an important fact about the Henselization of certain rings. Finally, in Section 4 we demonstrate the proof of Theorem 1.1 and present a new application of it, Theorem 4.3, in which we improve on the so-called Artin-Mazur lemma. We will recall all non-trivial definitions and try to be self-contained throughout the whole article.

Even though the proof of Theorem 1.1 is quite difficult, we can easily show it by the same trick as Furstenberg for a subclass of algebraic power series, which we call étale-algebraic. As we will see, the difficulty is then reducing the general case to the étale-algebraic one. This is done by proving that any algebraic power series can be represented as a rational function in an étale-algebraic series.

Definition.

An algebraic power series h⁡(x)∈K​⟨x⟩h(x)\in K\langle x\rangle with minimal polynomial P⁡(x,t)∈K⁡[x,t]P(x,t)\in K[x,t] is called étale-algebraic if h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0 and ∂tP⁡(0,0)≠0\partial_{t}P(0,0)\neq 0.

Note that it immediately follows from the implicit function theorem that the minimal polynomial (as a function in tt) of an étale-algebraic power series has a unique power series root vanishing at 00, which must be the étale-algebraic series itself. Therefore, étale-algebraic power series are exactly those series which are encoded uniquely by their minimal polynomial.

Example: Take x=x1x=x_{1}; the algebraic power series h~​(x)=x​1−x\tilde{h}(x)=x\sqrt{1-x} has minimal polynomial P~​(x,t)=t2+x3−x2\tilde{P}(x,t)=t^{2}+x^{3}-x^{2} which admits ∂tP~​(0,0)=0\partial_{t}\tilde{P}(0,0)=0 and therefore h~​(x)\tilde{h}(x) is not étale-algebraic. Clearly, P~​(x,t)=(t−x​1−x)​(t+x​1−x)\tilde{P}(x,t)=(t-x\sqrt{1-x})(t+x\sqrt{1-x}) has two power series solutions, both vanishing at 00. However, consider h⁡(x)=1−x−1h(x)=\sqrt{1-x}-1. Then still h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0 and for the new minimal polynomial we find ∂tP⁡(0,0)=2≠0\partial_{t}P(0,0)=2\neq 0, meaning that h⁡(x)h(x) is étale-algebraic.

Lemma 1.2.

Let h∈K​⟨x⟩h\in K\langle x\rangle be étale-algebraic with minimal polynomial P⁡(x,t)∈K⁡[x,t]P(x,t)\in K[x,t]. Then the following rational function is a power series

F≔t​∂tP⁡(x​t,t)P⁡(x​t,t)∈K⁡[[x,t]].\displaystyle F\coloneqq t\frac{\partial_{t}P(xt,t)}{P(xt,t)}\in K[\![x,t]\!].

Moreover, for any i∈ℕni\in\mathbb{N}^{n} and j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N}, the series xi​h​(x)jx^{i}h(x)^{j} is the diagonal of (x​t)i​tj+1​F(xt)^{i}t^{j+1}F. In particular, Theorem 1.1 holds if ff is étale-algebraic.

Proof.

Since h⁡(x)h(x) is a root of P⁡(x,t)P(x,t), we can write P⁡(x,t)=(t−h⁡(x))​Q​(x,t)P(x,t)=(t-h(x))Q(x,t) for some Q​(x,t)∈K​[[x]]​[t]Q(x,t)\in K[\![x]\!][t]. Differentiating both sides with respect to tt gives

∂tP⁡(x,t)=Q⁡(x,t)+(t−h⁡(x))​∂tQ⁡(x,t),\displaystyle\partial_{t}P(x,t)=Q(x,t)+(t-h(x))\partial_{t}Q(x,t), (1)

hence, after dividing through by P⁡(x,t)/tP(x,t)/t, we obtain

t​∂tP⁡(x,t)P⁡(x,t)=tt−h⁡(x)+t​∂tQ⁡(x,t)Q⁡(x,t).\displaystyle t\frac{\partial_{t}P(x,t)}{P(x,t)}=\frac{t}{t-h(x)}+t\frac{\partial_{t}Q(x,t)}{Q(x,t)}. (2)

Equation (1)(\ref{1}) implies that Q⁡(0,0)≠0Q(0,0)\neq 0, therefore Q⁡(x,t)∈K​[[x,t]]∗Q(x,t)\in K[\![x,t]\!]^{*} and consequently the second summand in the equation above is a power series. Furthermore, since h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0, we have

tt−h⁡(x​t)=11−t−1​h​(x​t)∈K⁡[[x,t]].\displaystyle\frac{t}{t-h(xt)}=\frac{1}{1-t^{-1}h(xt)}\in K[\![x,t]\!].

This concludes, using equation (2), the proof of the first part of the Lemma. For the second part, consider

R⁡(x,t)=(x​t)i​tj+1​∂tP⁡(x​t,t)P⁡(x​t,t).R(x,t)=(xt)^{i}t^{j+1}\frac{\partial_{t}P(xt,t)}{P(xt,t)}.

A straightforward computation together with equation (2) yields

𝒟⁡(R⁡(x,t))=𝒟⁡((x​t)i​tj​11−t−1​h​(x​t))=𝒟⁡((x​t)i​∑k≥0tj−k​h​(x​t)k)=𝒟⁡((x​t)i​h​(x​t)j)=xi​h​(x)j.\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathcal{D}(R(x,t))&=\mathcal{D}\Bigl((xt)^{i}t^{j}\frac{1}{1-t^{-1}h(xt)}\Bigr)=\mathcal{D}\Bigl((xt)^{i}\sum_{k\geq 0}t^{j-k}h(xt)^{k}\Bigr)\\ &=\mathcal{D}\bigl((xt)^{i}h(xt)^{j}\bigr)=x^{i}h(x)^{j}.\end{split} (3)

Finally, by setting i=0i=0 and j=1j=1 in (3), we obtain the theorem of Denef and Lipshitz for étale-algebraic power series. ∎

Now we dive into a more fundamental and basic study of our ring of interest K​⟨x⟩K\langle x\rangle.

1.2 Weierstrass Theorems

The Weierstrass division theorem (WDT) and the preparation theorem (WPT) are fundamental classical results about the rings of formal and convergent power series. WDT is in some sense a form of the Euclidean division algorithm, but requires an extra property on the divisor. Often, applications and implications of the division algorithm for the polynomial ring can be translated via the Weierstrass division theorem to K⁡[[x]]K[\![x]\!]. For example, it implies that the ring of formal power series is Noetherian, Henselian and a unique factorization domain. However, our main interest lies in the fact that both WDT and WPT hold true for algebraic power series and yield the same implications also for this ring. This fact was first proven by Lafon in 1965 [Laf65] and is much less known. We shall reprove it following the ideas from [LT70].

Definition.

We introduce the following notation and object:

  1. (1)

    The order of a non-zero formal power series f=∑α∈ℕnaα​xαf=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{n}}a_{\alpha}x^{\alpha}, denoted by ord​(f)\text{ord}(f), is the smallest integer d≥0d\geq 0 such that aα≠0a_{\alpha}\neq 0 for some α∈ℕn\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{n} with |α|=d|\alpha|=d. For f=0f=0 we say that ord​(f)=+∞\text{ord}(f)=+\infty.

  2. (2)

    A power series g∈K⁡[[x]]g\in K[\![x]\!] is called xnx_{n}-regular of order dd if g⁡(0,…,0,xn)=xnd​f​(xn)g(0,\dots,0,x_{n})=x_{n}^{d}f(x_{n}) for some power series f⁡(xn)∈K⁡[[xn]]f(x_{n})\in K[\![x_{n}]\!] with f⁡(0)≠0f(0)\neq 0.

  3. (3)

    A polynomial p∈K⁡[[x′]]​[xn]p\in K[\![x^{\prime}]\!][x_{n}] is called distinguished if it is of the form p=xnd+ad−1​(x′)​xnd−1+⋯+a0​(x′)p=x_{n}^{d}+a_{d-1}(x^{\prime})x_{n}^{d-1}+\cdots+a_{0}(x^{\prime}) for some power series ai​(x′)∈K⁡[[x′]]a_{i}(x^{\prime})\in K[\![x^{\prime}]\!] with ai​(0)=0a_{i}(0)=0 for i=0,…,d−1i=0,\dots,d-1.

Theorem 1.3 (WPT).

Let g∈K⁡[[x]]g\in K[\![x]\!] be an xnx_{n}-regular power series of order dd. Then there exist a unique p∈K⁡[[x′]]​[xn]p\in K[\![x^{\prime}]\!][x_{n}] which is a distinguished polynomial in xnx_{n} of degree dd and a unique unit u∈K​[[x]]∗u\in K[\![x]\!]^{*}, such that g=u​pg=up.

Theorem 1.4 (WDT).

Let g∈K⁡[[x]]g\in K[\![x]\!] be an xnx_{n}-regular power series of order dd. For any f∈K⁡[[x]]f\in K[\![x]\!] there exist uniquely a power series q∈K⁡[[x]]q\in K[\![x]\!] and an r∈K⁡[[x′]]​[xn]r\in K[\![x^{\prime}]\!][x_{n}] which is a distinguished polynomial in xnx_{n} of degree less than dd, such that f=q​g+rf=qg+r.

There are several different known ways to prove these classical theorems. The standard literature for their proofs and implications is the book “The Basic Theory of Power Series” by Ruiz [Rui93], a more recent and very short proof can be found in [Hau17]. A very explicit approach is followed by Lang in [Lan84]. Now we state and prove Lafon’s algebraic versions of these theorems.

Theorem 1.5 (Algebraic WPT).

Let g∈K​⟨x⟩g\in K\langle x\rangle be an xnx_{n}-regular algebraic power series of order dd. Then there exist a unique p∈K​⟨x′⟩​[xn]p\in K\langle x^{\prime}\rangle[x_{n}] which is a distinguished polynomial in xnx_{n} of degree dd with coefficients given by algebraic power series in x′x^{\prime} and a unique unit u∈K​⟨x⟩∗u\in K\langle x\rangle^{*}, such that g=u​pg=up.

Proof.

First note that we may assume without loss of generality that gg is irreducible as a power series. Write g=u​pg=up with u∈K​[[x]]∗u\in K[\![x]\!]^{*} and p∈K⁡[[x′]]​[x]p\in K[\![x^{\prime}]\!][x] a distinguished polynomial of degree dd. It follows that pp has dd distinct roots in an algebraic closure of the quotient ring of the formal power series Ω=Frac​(K​[[x′]])¯\Omega=\overline{\text{Frac}(K[\![x^{\prime}]\!])}, say α1,…,αd\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{d}. Now let G⁡(x,t)=G0​(x)+G1​(x)​t+⋯+Ge​(x)​te∈K⁡[x,t]G(x,t)=G_{0}(x)+G_{1}(x)t+\cdots+G_{e}(x)t^{e}\in K[x,t], G0≠0G_{0}\neq 0 be a minimal polynomial of gg, i.e. we have

0=G⁡(x,g⁡(x))=G0​(x)+G1​(x)​g​(x)+⋯+Ge​(x)​g​(x)e.\displaystyle 0=G(x,g(x))=G_{0}(x)+G_{1}(x)g(x)+\cdots+G_{e}(x)g(x)^{e}.

For every i=1,…,di=1,\dots,d we can replace xx by (x′,αi)(x^{\prime},\alpha_{i}) and, using g⁡(x′,αi)=0g(x^{\prime},\alpha_{i})=0, we obtain for every of those ii’s

0=G⁡(x′,αi,g⁡(x′,αi))=G0​(x′,αi).\displaystyle 0=G(x^{\prime},\alpha_{i},g(x^{\prime},\alpha_{i}))=G_{0}(x^{\prime},\alpha_{i}).

As 0≢G0​(x′,xn)∈K⁡[x′,xn]⊆K⁡(x′,xn)0\not\equiv G_{0}(x^{\prime},x_{n})\in K[x^{\prime},x_{n}]\subseteq K(x^{\prime},x_{n}) and annihilates αi\alpha_{i}, we get that αi\alpha_{i} is algebraic over K⁡(x′)K(x^{\prime}). It follows that xn−αix_{n}-\alpha_{i} is algebraic over K⁡(x′,xn)=K⁡(x)K(x^{\prime},x_{n})=K(x). Therefore, p=∏j=1d(xn−αj)p=\prod_{j=1}^{d}(x_{n}-\alpha_{j}) is an algebraic power series and the same holds for u=g/pu=g/p. Uniqueness is guaranteed by uniqueness of Weierstrass formal preparation (Theorem 1.3). ∎

Theorem 1.6 (Algebraic WDT).

Let g∈K​⟨x⟩g\in K\langle x\rangle be an xnx_{n}-regular algebraic power series of order dd. For any f∈K​⟨x⟩f\in K\langle x\rangle there exist uniquely an algebraic power series q∈K​⟨x⟩q\in K\langle x\rangle and an r∈K​⟨x′⟩​[xn]r\in K\langle x^{\prime}\rangle[x_{n}] which is a distinguished polynomial in xnx_{n} of degree less than dd with coefficients given by algebraic power series in x′x^{\prime}, such that f=q​g+rf=qg+r.

Proof.

Again, we may assume that gg is irreducible and by the algebraic Weierstrass preparation theorem, we may also assume without loss of generality that g∈K​⟨x′⟩​[xn]g\in K\langle x^{\prime}\rangle[x_{n}] is a distinguished polynomial of degree dd. We can divide formally:

f=q​g+r=q​g+∑j=0d−1bj​(x′)​xnj,\displaystyle f=qg+r=qg+\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}b_{j}(x^{\prime})x_{n}^{j}, (4)

for q∈K⁡[[x]]q\in K[\![x]\!] and b0​(x′),b1​(x′),…,bd−1​(x′)∈K⁡[[x′]]b_{0}(x^{\prime}),b_{1}(x^{\prime}),\dots,b_{d-1}(x^{\prime})\in K[\![x^{\prime}]\!] formal power series. Because gg is assumed to be a distinguished polynomial, we may write g=∑j=0dcj​(x′)​xnjg=\sum_{j=0}^{d}c_{j}(x^{\prime})x_{n}^{j} for some c0​(x′),…,cd​(x′)∈K⁡⟨x′⟩c_{0}(x^{\prime}),\dots,c_{d}(x^{\prime})\in K\langle x^{\prime}\rangle algebraic power series. We get that gg has dd distinct roots in Ω=Frac​(K​[[x′]])¯\Omega=\overline{\text{Frac}(K[\![x^{\prime}]\!])}, say α1,…,αd\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{d}. From (4)(\ref{fqgr}), by replacing xnx_{n} with αi\alpha_{i}, we get for every i=1,…,di=1,\dots,d that f⁡(x′,αi)=∑j=0d−1bj​(x′)​αijf(x^{\prime},\alpha_{i})=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}b_{j}(x^{\prime})\alpha_{i}^{j}. This can be rephrased in terms of a matrix multiplication:

(f⁡(x′,α1)f⁡(x′,αd))=(1α1⋯α1d−11α2⋯α2d−1⋱1αd⋯αdd−1)​(b0​(x′)bd−1​(x′)).\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}f(x^{\prime},\alpha_{1})\\ \vdots\\ f(x^{\prime},\alpha_{d})\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\alpha_{1}&\cdots&\alpha_{1}^{d-1}\\ 1&\alpha_{2}&\cdots&\alpha_{2}^{d-1}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ 1&\alpha_{d}&\cdots&\alpha_{d}^{d-1}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}b_{0}(x^{\prime})\\ \vdots\\ b_{d-1}(x^{\prime})\end{pmatrix}.

The matrix above is the Vandermonde matrix and it is invertible since the αi\alpha_{i}’s are pairwise different. Therefore, each bi​(x′)b_{i}(x^{\prime}) is uniquely given by some rational expression in the f⁡(x′,αj)f(x^{\prime},\alpha_{j})’s and αk\alpha_{k}’s for j,k∈{1,…,d}j,k\in\{1,\dots,d\}. On the other hand, by the same argument as in the proof of Theorem 1.5, we obtain that each αi\alpha_{i} is algebraic over K⁡(x′)K(x^{\prime}). Moreover, by assumption f⁡(x′,xn)f(x^{\prime},x_{n}) is algebraic over K⁡(x′,xn)K(x^{\prime},x_{n}). It follows that both field extensions K⁡(x′)⊆K⁡(x′,αi)K(x^{\prime})\subseteq K(x^{\prime},\alpha_{i}) and K⁡(x′,αi)⊆K⁡(x′,αi,f⁡(x′,αi))K(x^{\prime},\alpha_{i})\subseteq K(x^{\prime},\alpha_{i},f(x^{\prime},\alpha_{i})) are finite. Hence, K⁡(x′)⊆K⁡(x′,f⁡(x′,αi))K(x^{\prime})\subseteq K(x^{\prime},f(x^{\prime},\alpha_{i})) is finite and consequently f⁡(x′,αi)f(x^{\prime},\alpha_{i}) is algebraic over K⁡(x′)K(x^{\prime}). As this holds for every i=1,…,di=1,\dots,d, it follows that also any rational expression in the f⁡(x′,αj)f(x^{\prime},\alpha_{j})’s and αk\alpha_{k}’s for j,k∈{1,…,d}j,k\in\{1,\dots,d\} is algebraic over K⁡(x′)K(x^{\prime}). Recall that each bi​(x′)b_{i}(x^{\prime}) is such an expression, therefore each bi​(x′)b_{i}(x^{\prime}) is algebraic over K⁡(x′)K(x^{\prime}) and hence an algebraic power series. It follows that r=∑j=0d−1bj​(x′)​xnjr=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}b_{j}(x^{\prime})x_{n}^{j} is an algebraic power series and finally the same holds for q=(f−r)/gq=(f-r)/g. Uniqueness is clear by the formal WDT (Theorem 1.4). ∎

As already mentioned, this theorem has many implications. For example, the proofs from [Rui93] and [Lan84] that K⁡[[x]]K[\![x]\!] is Noetherian and a UFD can be directly carried out for K​⟨x⟩K\langle x\rangle. Another corollary is the following:

Theorem 1.7 (Hensel’s Lemma).

Let f∈K​⟨x⟩​[t]f\in K\langle x\rangle[t] be a monic polynomial in tt over K​⟨x⟩K\langle x\rangle. Assume α∈K\alpha\in K is a root of multiplicity dd of the polynomial f⁡(0,t)∈K⁡[t]f(0,t)\in K[t]. Then there exist unique monic polynomials p,u∈K​⟨x⟩​[t]p,u\in K\langle x\rangle[t] with u⁡(0,α)≠0u(0,\alpha)\neq 0, pp of degree dd in tt, p⁡(0,t)=(t−α)dp(0,t)=(t-\alpha)^{d} and f=u​pf=up.

Proof.

After the change of the variable tt to t+αt+\alpha, we may assume that α=0\alpha=0. Since α\alpha is a dd-multiple root of f⁡(0,t)f(0,t), it follows that f⁡(x,t)f(x,t) is tt-regular of order dd. By the algebraic WPT in n+1n+1 variables we may write uniquely f=u​pf=up where p∈K​⟨x⟩​[t]p\in K\langle x\rangle[t] is a distinguished polynomial in tt of degree dd and u∈K​⟨x,t⟩∗u\in K\langle x,t\rangle^{*} a unit, hence u⁡(0,α)=u⁡(0,0)≠0u(0,\alpha)=u(0,0)\neq 0. Moreover, since p⁡(x,t)p(x,t) is distinguished of degree dd it follows by definition that p⁡(0,t)=td=(t−α)dp(0,t)=t^{d}=(t-\alpha)^{d}. u⁡(x,t)∈K​⟨x⟩​[t]u(x,t)\in K\langle x\rangle[t] because of polynomial division in this ring. Uniqueness follows from the uniqueness of the algebraic Weierstrass division theorem. ∎

The statement above ensures that a root α∈K\alpha\in K of f⁡(0,t)f(0,t) gives rise to a factorization f=u​pf=up. This factorization is called the lifting of α\alpha. Lifting all roots separately, one by one, it is possible to prove that coprime factorizations can be lifted as well.

Theorem 1.8 (Hensel’s Lemma).

Let f∈K​⟨x⟩​[t]f\in K\langle x\rangle[t] be a monic polynomial in tt over K​⟨x⟩K\langle x\rangle. Assume f​(0,t)=p¯​(t)​q¯​(t)f(0,t)=\bar{p}(t)\bar{q}(t) factors into two monic coprime polynomials. Then there exist two unique monic polynomials p,q∈K​⟨x⟩​[t]p,q\in K\langle x\rangle[t] with p​(0,t)=p¯​(t)p(0,t)=\bar{p}(t), q​(0,t)=q¯​(t)q(0,t)=\bar{q}(t) and f=q​pf=qp.

We omit the detailed proof here, because the equivalence on these two versions of Hensel’s lemma will be justified in Section 3 in a more general setting. Instead, we explain the importance of these theorems following the motivation in [Eis95, pp. 185].

1.3 The Importance of Hensel’s Lemma

Consider the nodal plane cubic curve over a field KK (of characteristic 00 as always or positive but not equal to 22) given by the equation t2−x2​(1+x)=0t^{2}-x^{2}(1+x)=0 for x=x1x=x_{1}. The associated affine coordinate ring is S=K⁡[x,t]/(t2−x2​(1+x))S=K[x,t]/(t^{2}-x^{2}(1+x)). Of course, the curve is irreducible and SS is a domain. When looking at the picture over ℝ\mathbb{R} (Figure 1), one may think that localizing SS at the maximal ideal 𝔪=(x¯,t¯)\mathfrak{m}=(\bar{x},\bar{t}) will make the ring have zero divisors, however this is not the case: every Zariski neighborhood of 00 of the node is irreducible. The reason is that over the complex numbers a neighborhood of the omitted origin is a punctured disc and therefore the curve remains irreducible. We would still like to factor t2−x2​(1+x)t^{2}-x^{2}(1+x) somehow, in order to study the easier rings into which SS will decompose. Examining a “really small neighborhood” of the node, we would expect the curve to become reducible there: for example over the ring of formal power series the expression t2−x2​(1+x)t^{2}-x^{2}(1+x) is in fact reducible. This comes from the fact that 1+x1+x has a square root in K⁡[[x]]K[\![x]\!] and we may therefore write

t2−x2​(1+x)=(t−x​1+x)​(t+x​1+x)t^{2}-x^{2}(1+x)=(t-x\sqrt{1+x})(t+x\sqrt{1+x}). One can argue the reason why it is immediately clear that 1+x1+x is a square over K⁡[[x]]K[\![x]\!] is that this ring satisfies Hensel’s lemma! More precisely, take the polynomial f⁡(x,t)=t2−(1+x)f(x,t)=t^{2}-(1+x), then f⁡(0,t)=(t−1)​(t+1)=p¯​(t)​q¯​(t)f(0,t)=(t-1)(t+1)=\bar{p}(t)\bar{q}(t) and these polynomials are coprime. Therefore, by Hensel’s lemma, this factorization must admit a lifting and therefore 1+x∈K⁡[[x]]\sqrt{1+x}\in K[\![x]\!]. This is also the reason why we explicitly do not allow the characteristic of KK to be 22: in this case p¯​(t)\bar{p}(t) and q¯​(t)\bar{q}(t) would not be relatively prime and the lifting would not be guaranteed, in fact it would not exist. However, we also see that in order to make the node reducible, we do not have to go from K⁡[x,t]K[x,t] all the way up to the polynomial ring over the completion K​[[x]]​[t]K[\![x]\!][t]: it suffices to take any Henselian ring extension of SS or of K​[x](x)K[x]_{(x)}. This is exactly the idea and motivation for defining the Henselization.

2 Algebraic Power Series and Henselization

The main goal of this section is to stress the connection between the algebraic closure in the completion of a ring and the property of being Henselian, that is to satisfy Hensel’s lemma. We will be able to prove that, under certain conditions, any Henselian ring is algebraically closed in its completion, that is, if a∈R^a\in\widehat{R} is algebraic over a Henselian RR then it must already hold that a∈Ra\in R. This will allow us to look at the ring of algebraic power series from a different viewpoint. The conditions may appear technical at first sight, however they have the purpose of excluding pathologies while still allowing for a large class of rings. A considerably different approach to this theory can be found in the book [KPR75] by Kurke, Pfister and Roczen.

We will work with local rings, i.e with those rings RR, which have exactly one maximal ideal. Usually, we will denote this maximal ideal by 𝔪\mathfrak{m} and let K≔R/𝔪K\coloneqq R/\mathfrak{m} be the residue field with respect to 𝔪\mathfrak{m}. Sometimes, we write triples (R,𝔪,K)(R,\mathfrak{m},K) when talking about local rings, combining these three objects. It is immediate to see that RR has only one maximal ideal 𝔪\mathfrak{m} if and only if R∗=R∖𝔪R^{*}=R\setminus\mathfrak{m}. Recall that given two local rings (R,𝔪,K),(S,𝔫,L)(R,\mathfrak{m},K),(S,\mathfrak{n},L), a homomorphism ϕ:R→S\phi:R\to S is called local if ϕ⁡(𝔪)⊆𝔫\phi(\mathfrak{m})\subseteq\mathfrak{n} holds and this condition is equivalent to ϕ−1​(𝔫)=𝔪\phi^{-1}(\mathfrak{n})=\mathfrak{m}. Note that both, the rings of formal and algebraic power series, are local with maximal ideal 𝔪=(x)=(x1,…,xn)\mathfrak{m}=(x)=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}). It is also obvious that the residue field K⁡[[x]]/(x)≅K⁡⟨x⟩/(x)K[\![x]\!]/(x)\cong K\langle x\rangle/(x) is (isomorphic to) KK. Recall that the completion of a local ring (R,𝔪,K)(R,\mathfrak{m},K) is defined as the inverse limit lim←⁡R/𝔪i\varprojlim R/\mathfrak{m}^{i}. A local ring (R,𝔪,K)(R,\mathfrak{m},K) is called complete if the canonical map to its completion R→R^R\to\widehat{R} is an isomorphism. Note that ∩i𝔪i\cap_{i}\mathfrak{m}^{i} goes to zero under this mapping, therefore completeness implies ∩i𝔪i=0\cap_{i}\mathfrak{m}^{i}=0. Krull’s intersection theorem justifies that the completion of a Noetherian ring (i.e. a ring with only finitely generated ideals) is complete, however this is false in general. Finally, recall that the completion R^\widehat{R} of RR satisfies the universal property that for any local (R,𝔪)→(S,𝔫)(R,\mathfrak{m})\to(S,\mathfrak{n}) with (S,𝔫)(S,\mathfrak{n}) complete there exists a unique factorization R→R^→SR\to\widehat{R}\to S.

2.1 Henselian Rings

Given a p∈R⁡[t]p\in R[t], we will denote by p¯∈K⁡[t]\bar{p}\in K[t] the reduction of pp mod 𝔪​R​[t]\mathfrak{m}R[t], given by reducing all coefficients of pp mod 𝔪\mathfrak{m}.

Definition.

A local ring (R,𝔪,K)(R,\mathfrak{m},K) is called Henselian if the following property holds:
Let f⁡(t)∈R⁡[t]f(t)\in R[t] be a monic polynomial. Assume that f¯​(t)=p0​(t)​q0​(t)\bar{f}(t)=p_{0}(t)q_{0}(t) holds for two monic coprime polynomials p0​(t),q0​(t)∈K⁡[t]{p_{0}}(t),q_{0}(t)\in K[t]. Then there exist two unique monic polynomials p⁡(t),q⁡(t)∈R⁡[t]p(t),q(t)\in R[t] satisfying p¯​(t)=p0​(t),q¯​(t)=q0​(t)\bar{p}(t)=p_{0}(t),\bar{q}(t)=q_{0}(t), deg⁡p⁡(t)=deg⁡p0​(t)\deg p(t)=\deg p_{0}(t), deg⁡q⁡(t)=deg⁡q0​(t)\deg q(t)=\deg q_{0}(t) and f⁡(t)=p⁡(t)​q​(t)f(t)=p(t)q(t).

The notion of Henselian rings (or Hensel rings) was first introduced by Azumaya in [Azu51]. The property above is usually referred to as “Hensel’s lemma” even though it is used as a definition. One often reads in the literature “A ring is called Henselian, if Hensel’s lemma holds [in this ring]”. To avoid confusion, we will call the statement above Hensel’s property. The actual “lemma” of Hensel is the following classical theorem (see for example [Eis95, Chapter 7]):

Theorem 2.1 (Hensel’s lemma for complete rings).

Let (R,𝔪,K)(R,\mathfrak{m},K) be a complete local ring. Then RR is Henselian.

Standard references for Henselian rings are [Nag62, Ray70, Gro67]. For the purpose of this work, a very significant fact is that Theorem 1.8 implies the following:

Theorem 2.2.

The ring of algebraic power series K​⟨x⟩K\langle x\rangle is Henselian.

Another key fact about Henselian rings is the following lemma. Its statement and proof appear in [Nag62] and give an introductory flavor to this section. Recall that given an extension of rings R⊆SR\subseteq S, an element s∈Ss\in S is called integral over RR if there exists a monic polynomial P⁡(t)∈R⁡[t]P(t)\in R[t] with P⁡(s)=0P(s)=0. The extension is said to be integral if this holds for any s∈Ss\in S.

Lemma 2.3.

Let RR be a Henselian integral domain and R′R^{\prime} an integral extension of RR. Then R′R^{\prime} is a local ring.

Proof.

Let 𝔪\mathfrak{m} be the maximal ideal of RR and assume that R′R^{\prime} has two maximal ideals 𝔪1′≠𝔪2′\mathfrak{m}_{1}^{\prime}\neq\mathfrak{m}_{2}^{\prime}. Take some a∈𝔪1′a\in\mathfrak{m}_{1}^{\prime} which is not in 𝔪2′\mathfrak{m}_{2}^{\prime}. We have an irreducible monic polynomial f⁡(t)=tn+cn−1​tn−1+⋯+c0∈R⁡[t]f(t)=t^{n}+c_{n-1}t^{n-1}+\cdots+c_{0}\in R[t] which has aa as root. Now, as a∈𝔪1′a\in\mathfrak{m}_{1}^{\prime}, we must have c0∈𝔪1′∩R⊆𝔪c_{0}\in\mathfrak{m}_{1}^{\prime}\cap R\subseteq\mathfrak{m}. We also have that an∉𝔪​R​[a]a^{n}\not\in\mathfrak{m}R[a], because a∉𝔪2′a\not\in\mathfrak{m}_{2}^{\prime}, hence there must be a cic_{i} which is not in 𝔪\mathfrak{m}. Take j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N} such that cj∉𝔪c_{j}\not\in\mathfrak{m} but cj−s∈𝔪c_{j-s}\in\mathfrak{m} for 0<s≤j0<s\leq j. Clearly 1≤j≤n−11\leq j\leq n-1 and we have

f⁡(t)≡(tj+cn−1​tj−1+⋯+cn−j)​tn−jmod𝔪​R​[t].f(t)\equiv(t^{j}+c_{n-1}t^{j-1}+\cdots+c_{n-j})t^{n-j}\mod\mathfrak{m}R[t].

But this means that the image of ff is reducible mod 𝔪​R​[t]\mathfrak{m}R[t] and using that RR is Henselian we obtain that ff must be reducible in R⁡[t]R[t]. This is a contradiction and the assertion is proved. ∎

To state the main theorem of this section we will need some conditions on our local ring RR. Therefore we define the necessary terms:

Definition.

Let RR be a ring.

  1. (1)

    RR is called analytically irreducible if it is local and its completion R^\widehat{R} is a domain. RR is called analytically normal if it is local and R^\widehat{R} is normal44 4 Recall that a local ring is called normal if is integrally closed in its quotient field..

  2. (2)

    Assume RR be an integral domain with quotient field LL. RR is called Japanese55 5 According to [Sta20] this name was first used by Grothendieck in order to contribute to Nakayama, Takagi, Nagata and many others. if it satisfies the so-called finiteness condition for integral extensions. This means, for every finite extension L′L^{\prime} of the quotient field LL, the integral closure of RR in L′L^{\prime} is a finitely generated RR-module.

  3. (3)

    RR is called a Nagata ring66 6 In the book “Local Rings” Nagata calls these rings pseudo-geometric. if RR is Noetherian and for every prime ideal 𝔭⊆R\mathfrak{p}\subseteq R, the ring R/𝔭R/\mathfrak{p} is Japanese.

Lemma 2.4.

If RR is a Nagata ring, then every ring which is a finite module over RR or a ring of quotients of RR is also Nagata. Any localization of RR is also Nagata. Any finitely generated RR-algebra is Nagata.

We see that the category of Nagata rings is reasonably large and closed under many operations. Good references for the proofs of the lemma above are [Nag62, Section 36] and [Mat80, Section 31]. Of course, most facts can also be found in [Sta20, Section 032E].

Finally, for our purposes we need the following version of the Zariski Main Theorem, which is Theorem 37.8 in [Nag62]. Recall that SS is said to be of finite type over RR if SS is isomorphic to a quotient of R⁡[x1,…,xn]R[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] as an RR-algebra.

Lemma 2.5.

Let RR be an analytically normal ring. If a normal and local Nagata ring SS is of finite type over RR, then SS analytically irreducible.

We are ready to prove one central theorem of this section, connecting Henselian rings with the property of being algebraically closed in the completion, and which will be a crucial ingredient in the proof of Theorem 2.7. This theorem explains why the study of algebraic power series essentially comes down to studying Henselian rings. Its statement can be found in [Nag62, (44.1)], however the proof given there is very concise and in some places unclear. Therefore we shall reprove the theorem here.

Theorem 2.6.

Let RR be a Henselian, analytically normal Nagata ring. Then RR is algebraically closed in its completion, i.e. if a∈R^a\in\widehat{R} algebraic over RR, then a∈Ra\in R.

Proof.

Let aa be an element of R^\widehat{R} which is algebraic over RR. Then we can find b≠0b\neq 0 in RR such that c≔a​bc\coloneqq ab is integral over RR. We claim that R⁡[c]=RR[c]=R. Assume otherwise and let f∈R⁡[t]f\in R[t] be the minimal polynomial of cc. We wish to use the lemma above on R⁡[c]R[c], but we lack the assumption of normality. So we define R′R^{\prime} to be the integral closure of R⁡[c]R[c] in L⁡[c]L[c], where L=Frac​(R)L=\text{Frac}(R), so R′R^{\prime} is normal by definition. By an easy observation it follows that R′R^{\prime} is also the integral closure of RR in L⁡[c]L[c]. Since RR is analytically normal, it is a domain and therefore the ideal (0)(0) is prime. By the definition of a Nagata ring, it follows that the integral closure of R=R/(0)R=R/(0) in any finite extension of LL is a finitely generated RR-module. Since cc is integral and in particular algebraic, it follows that L⁡[c]L[c] is a finite extension of LL and therefore R′R^{\prime} is a finitely generated RR-module. Furthermore, R′R^{\prime}, being finitely generated over a Nagata ring, is still Nagata by Proposition 2.4 and also R′R^{\prime} is indeed local by Lemma 2.377 7 This is where we use the Henselian assumption., hence we may apply Lemma 2.5 to get that R′R^{\prime} is analytically irreducible. However, we have that R′^=R′⊗RR^\widehat{R^{\prime}}=R^{\prime}\otimes_{R}\widehat{R} and this must be a domain. Now look at the completion of R⁡[c]R[c], which is given by R⁡[c]⊗RR^R[c]\otimes_{R}\widehat{R}. Now, R→R^R\to\widehat{R} is flat, meaning that we also have the inclusion R⁡[c]⊗RR^⊆R′⊗RR^R[c]\otimes_{R}\widehat{R}\subseteq R^{\prime}\otimes_{R}\widehat{R} and hence R⁡[c]^\widehat{R[c]} must be a domain as well. On the other hand, we have R⁡[c]^=R⁡[c]⊗RR^=R^​[t]/(f)\widehat{R[c]}=R[c]\otimes_{R}\widehat{R}=\widehat{R}[t]/(f), identifying ff with its image in R^​[t]\widehat{R}[t]. However c∈R^c\in\widehat{R} is a root of ff, hence R^​[t]/(f)\widehat{R}[t]/(f) cannot be a domain: a contradiction. So c∈Rc\in R and hence a∈Frac​(R)a\in\text{Frac}(R). Because R=Frac​(R)∩R^R=\text{Frac}(R)\cap\widehat{R} and since aa is in both rings, we get that a∈Ra\in R as wanted. ∎

2.2 Henselian Characterization of Algebraic Power Series

We saw that Henselian rings are closely connected to algebraic closures in the completion. In particular, at this point, one may conjecture that for some, not necessarily Henselian, ring RR, if we can define the “smallest” Henselian extension of RR, it will be exactly the algebraic closure of RR in R^\widehat{R}. Since algebraic power series are by definition the algebraic closure of K​[x](x)K[x]_{(x)} in its completion, this approach will also give a different viewpoint on our main ring of interest. Note that obviously any field is Nagata, therefore by Lemma 2.4 it follows that K⁡[x]K[x] is also a Nagata ring. Then K​[x](x)K[x]_{(x)} is again Nagata, since it is a localization.

Definition.

Let (R,𝔪,K)(R,\mathfrak{m},K) be a local ring. We say a Henselian ring RhR^{\text{h}} together with a local homomorphism i:R→Rhi:R\to R^{\text{h}} is the Henselization of RR, if any local homomorphism from RR to a Henselian ring factors uniquely through ii.

In other words, the Henselian ring RhR^{\text{h}} together with i:R→Rhi:R\to R^{\text{h}} is the Henselization of RR, if for any Henselian ring HH and local ψ:R→H\psi:R\to H there exists a unique local ϕ\phi such that the following diagram commutes:

This notion was first introduced by Nagata in the article “On the theory of Henselian rings”, which became the first of a trilogy [Nag53, Nag54, Nag59]. Since then, the Henselization of a ring became a very well studied object; we shall only explain those facts which are of importance for our purpose.

Note that from the definition it follows that if RhR^{\text{h}} exists, then it must be unique up to isomorphism. For Noetherian rings one has the inclusion R↪R^R\hookrightarrow\widehat{R}; this together with Hensel’s lemma immediately implies that ii must be injective as well in this case. Moreover, the following fact follows also easily from the universal property: Assume the existence of a Henselian ring R′R^{\prime} such that R⊆R′⊆RhR\subseteq R^{\prime}\subseteq R^{\text{h}}, then R′=RhR^{\prime}=R^{\text{h}}. In this sense we can view the Henselization as the “smallest” Henselian ring extension of RR. Note that it is not obvious that RhR^{\text{h}} exists for any local RR, however this is true and we will prove this in the next section (Section 3.3).

The following theorem allows a purely ring-theoretic viewpoint on K​⟨x⟩K\langle x\rangle.

Theorem 2.7.

Let R=K​[x](x)R=K[x]_{(x)} be the localization of K⁡[x]K[x] at the maximal ideal (x)(x). Assume that the Henselization of RR exists88 8 In the next section (Section 3.3) we will prove that the Henselization of a local ring always exists.. Then it is isomorphic to the ring of algebraic power series: Rh≅K​⟨x⟩R^{\text{h}}\cong K\langle x\rangle.

For the proof we need two lemmas: we provide a proof for the first, and a reference for the second.

Lemma 2.8.

Let RhR^{\text{h}} be the Henselization of a Noetherian local ring RR. Then Rh^=R^\widehat{R^{\text{h}}}=\widehat{R}.

Proof.

By Hensel’s lemma R^\widehat{R} is Henselian, thus there exists a unique factorization R→Rh→R^R\to R^{\text{h}}\to\widehat{R}. Let SS be a complete local ring with maximal ideal 𝔫\mathfrak{n} and assume Rh→SR^{\text{h}}\to S is a local map. Precomposing with ii gives R→Rh→SR\to R^{\text{h}}\to S. By the universal property of the completion and then by the factorization of R→R^R\to\widehat{R} we also find R→Rh→R^→SR\to R^{\text{h}}\to\widehat{R}\to S. Now, since SS being complete is also Henselian, the uniqueness in the universal property of RhR^{\text{h}} implies that these factorizations are equal. Hence, for every R→SR\to S with SS complete we find Rh→R^→SR^{\text{h}}\to\widehat{R}\to S. The universal property of the completion forces Rh^=R^\widehat{R^{\text{h}}}=\widehat{R}. ∎

Lemma 2.9.

Let RR be a local Nagata ring. Then its Henselization RhR^{\text{h}} is also Nagata. Moreover, if RR is also analytically normal then so is RhR^{\text{h}}.

For the proof see [Nag62, (44.2,44.3)].

Proof of Theorem 2.7.

By Lemma 2.9 it follows that K​[x](x)hK[x]_{(x)}^{\text{h}} is both analytically normal and Nagata. Because the ring of algebraic power series is Henselian (Theorem 2.2) and the Henselization is the smallest Henselian ring extension of a given ring, it suffices to show K⁡⟨x⟩⊆K​[x](x)hK\langle x\rangle\subseteq K[x]_{(x)}^{\text{h}}. Let f∈K⁡⟨x⟩⊆K⁡[[x]]=K​[x](x)^f\in K\langle x\rangle\subseteq K[\![x]\!]=\widehat{K[x]_{(x)}}. Then obviously ff is algebraic over K​[x](x)hK[x]_{(x)}^{\text{h}} and by Lemma 2.8 we must have f∈K​[x](x)h^f\in\widehat{K[x]_{(x)}^{\text{h}}}. We can apply Theorem 2.6 to see that f∈K​[x](x)hf\in K[x]_{(x)}^{\text{h}}. ∎

3 Étale Ring Maps and Henselization

3.1 Motivation for Étale Ring Maps

Before giving the rigorous definition of an étale map R→SR\to S between two rings R,SR,S, we will try to explain the motivation behind it. Milne writes in his lecture notes [Mil13]:

“An étale morphism is the analogue in algebraic geometry of a local isomorphism of manifolds in differential geometry, a covering of Riemann surfaces with no branch points in complex analysis, and an unramified extension in algebraic number theory.”

Of course, the importance of these objects makes it clear that one needs a definition in the setting of algebraic geometry and that this definition might be involved. There are many equivalent ways to define this analogue and we will try to motivate the one that is mostly geometric and closest to a universal property.

Consider the case of two affine algebraic varieties X=V⁡(f1,…,fr)⊆Kn,Y=V⁡(g1,…,gs)⊆KmX=V(f_{1},\dots,f_{r})\subseteq K^{n},Y=V(g_{1},\dots,g_{s})\subseteq K^{m} and a morphism fϕ:X→Yf_{\phi}:X\to Y coming from ϕ:R→S\phi:R\to S, where

R≔K⁡[Y]\displaystyle R\coloneqq K[Y] =K⁡[y1,…,ym]/(g1,…,gs)​ and\displaystyle=K[y_{1},\dots,y_{m}]/(g_{1},\dots,g_{s})\text{ and }
S≔K⁡[X]\displaystyle S\coloneqq K[X] =K⁡[x1,…,xn]/(f1,…,fr)\displaystyle=K[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]/(f_{1},\dots,f_{r})

are the corresponding coordinate rings. Recall that a local diffeomorphism is characterized by its bijective differential. We want to achieve an analogous property for fϕf_{\phi} by putting only algebraic conditions on ϕ\phi.

By definition, fϕf_{\phi} maps any KK-point a≔(a1,…,an)∈Xa\coloneqq(a_{1},\dots,a_{n})\in X to a KK-point b≔(b1,…,bm)∈Yb\coloneqq(b_{1},\dots,b_{m})\in Y. To formulate this in an algebraic way, we can require the following diagram to commute:

To see that this algebraic formulation indeed corresponds to the geometric viewpoint of sending a∈Xa\in X to some b∈Yb\in Y, note that the map K⁡[X]→KK[X]\to K defines a KK-point of XX, since it maps each xix_{i} to aia_{i} for some a≔(a1,…,an)∈Kna\coloneqq(a_{1},\dots,a_{n})\in K^{n} with the condition that each fj​(a1,…,an)=0f_{j}(a_{1},\dots,a_{n})=0, 1≤j≤r1\leq j\leq r, hence, by definition, a∈Xa\in X. Similarly, K⁡[Y]→KK[Y]\to K is a KK-point, say b=(b1,…,bm)∈Yb=(b_{1},\dots,b_{m})\in Y, because gj​(b1,…,bm)=0g_{j}(b_{1},\dots,b_{m})=0 for j=1,…,sj=1,\dots,s. The commutativity of the diagram means that sending (y1,…,ym)↦(b1,…,bm)(y_{1},\dots,y_{m})\mapsto(b_{1},\dots,b_{m}) by the diagonal map is the same as sending (y1​…,ym)↦(ϕ1​(x1,…,xn),…,ϕm​(x1,…,xn))↦(ϕ1​(a),…,ϕm​(a))(y_{1}\dots,y_{m})\mapsto(\phi_{1}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}),\dots,\phi_{m}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))\mapsto(\phi_{1}(a),\dots,\phi_{m}(a)): KK-points are sent to KK-points.

Now we want to describe the behavior of fϕf_{\phi} on tangent vectors. We can formulate this in an algebraic way, by requiring the commutativity of the following diagram, adding the ring K⁡[ε]/(ε2)K[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^{2}) to the above:

Since

K⁡[Y]\displaystyle K[Y] →K⁡[ε]/(ε2)→K\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\hskip 28.45274pt}K[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^{2})\xrightarrow{\hskip 34.14322pt}K
(y1,…,ym)\displaystyle(y_{1},\dots,y_{m}) ↦(b1+ε​c1,…,bm+ε​cm)↦(b1,…,bm),\displaystyle\mapsto(b_{1}+\varepsilon c_{1},\dots,b_{m}+\varepsilon c_{m})\mapsto(b_{1},\dots,b_{m}),

we see that this intermediate ring does not destroy the considerations above. Moreover, we claim that the map K⁡[Y]→K⁡[ε]/(ε2)K[Y]\to K[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^{2}) corresponds to a tangent vector of YY: say, we have

K⁡[Y]=K⁡[y1,…,ym]/(g1,…,gs)\displaystyle K[Y]=K[y_{1},\dots,y_{m}]/(g_{1},\dots,g_{s}) →K⁡[ε]/(ε2)\displaystyle\to K[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^{2})
yi\displaystyle y_{i} ↦bi+ε​ci,1≤i≤m,\displaystyle\mapsto b_{i}+\varepsilon c_{i},\hskip 14.22636pt1\leq i\leq m,

for some b∈Kmb\in K^{m} and c≔(c1,…,cm)∈Kmc\coloneqq(c_{1},\dots,c_{m})\in K^{m}. Then it must hold that gj​(b1+ε​c1,…,bm+ε​cm)=0g_{j}(b_{1}+\varepsilon c_{1},\dots,b_{m}+\varepsilon c_{m})=0 for 1≤j≤s1\leq j\leq s. Using Taylor expansion and the fact that ε2=0\varepsilon^{2}=0 in K⁡[ε]/(ε2)K[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^{2}), we obtain:

0=gj​(b1+ε​c1,…,bm+ε​cm)=gj​(b)+∑i=1m∂gj∂yi​(b)​ci​ε.0=g_{j}(b_{1}+\varepsilon c_{1},\dots,b_{m}+\varepsilon c_{m})=g_{j}(b)+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\partial g_{j}}{\partial y_{i}}(b)c_{i}\varepsilon.

∑i=1m∂gj∂yi​(b)​ci=0,1≤j≤s.\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\partial g_{j}}{\partial y_{i}}(b)c_{i}=0,\hskip 14.22636pt1\leq j\leq s.

This is of course equivalent to c⋅∇gj​(b)=0c\cdot\nabla g_{j}(b)=0, i.e. cc is a tangent vector of YY at bb and we may say c∈Tb​Yc\in T_{b}Y, the tangent space of YY at bb.

Up to now, we have reformulated the property of fϕf_{\phi} to map KK-points to KK-points and added the potential of considering tangent vectors in terms of a commutative diagram. We can now add the final requirement to ϕ\phi, making it the analogue of a local diffeomorphism: we want its “differential” Ta​X→Tfϕ​(a)​Y=Tb​YT_{a}X\to T_{f_{\phi}(a)}Y=T_{b}Y to be bijective. Surprisingly, this condition is very easy to add in our commutative diagram formalism: we require additionally the existence and uniqueness of the diagonal arrow, preserving commutativity:

By the same argument as above, we can easily convince ourselves that this diagonal map writes K⁡[X]→K⁡[ε]/(ε2):xi↦ai+ε​diK[X]\to K[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^{2}):x_{i}\mapsto a_{i}+\varepsilon d_{i} for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n and some d≔(d1,…,dn)d\coloneqq(d_{1},\dots,d_{n}) which corresponds to a tangent vector of XX. The commutativity of the upper-right triangle just means that this vector is in the tangent space Ta​XT_{a}X. Finally, consider the commutativity of the lower triangle. On the one hand, we can map by the horizontal homomorphism yj↦bj+ε​cjy_{j}\mapsto b_{j}+\varepsilon c_{j}, 1≤j≤m1\leq j\leq m as we already saw. On the other hand, going the other path, we have again by Taylor’s expansion for j=1,…,mj=1,\dots,m:

yj↦ϕj​(x1,…,xn)↦ϕj​(a1+ε​d1,…,an+ε​dn)=ϕj​(a)+∑i=1n∂ϕj∂xi​(a)​di​ε.y_{j}\mapsto\phi_{j}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\mapsto\phi_{j}(a_{1}+\varepsilon d_{1},\dots,a_{n}+\varepsilon d_{n})=\phi_{j}(a)+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial\phi_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}(a)d_{i}\varepsilon.

Since the lower-left triangle commutes, we have by comparison of the coefficient of ε\varepsilon that

cj=∑i=1n∂ϕj∂xi​(a)​di,1≤j≤m.c_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial\phi_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}(a)d_{i},\hskip 14.22636pt1\leq j\leq m.

Putting these mm equations together, we define the Jacobian matrix

Jϕ​(a)≔(∂ϕj∂xi​(a))1≤i≤n1≤j≤m.J_{\phi}(a)\coloneqq\left(\frac{\partial\phi_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}(a)\right)_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i\leq n\\ 1\leq j\leq m\end{subarray}}.

Then, the equation above is, of course, equivalent to Jϕ​(a)​d=cJ_{\phi}(a)d=c.

Hence, the existence of the diagonal arrow makes sure that for any tangent vector at b∈Yb\in Y, we have at least one tangent vector at a∈Xa\in X mapping to it, in other words it ensures the surjectivity of Jϕ​(a)J_{\phi}(a). Analogously, the uniqueness of the diagonal map translates into injectivity of the differential. Equipped with this good understanding of what it means to define the algebraic analogue of a local diffeomorphism, we can step forward to its rigorous definition.

3.2 Étale Ring Maps

We will present only those results about étale ring maps that are important for the construction of the Henselization. For other statements and some omitted proofs we refer to standard literature such as [Mil80, Gro67, Ray70] and of course [Sta20, Section 00U0].

Definition.

Given an RR-algebra SS with the homomorphism ϕ:R→S\phi:R\to S, we call SS formally étale if the following condition is satisfied:
Suppose that TT is some RR-algebra, 𝔫⊆T\mathfrak{n}\subseteq T some ideal with 𝔫2=0\mathfrak{n}^{2}=0 and the following diagram of RR-algebra maps commutes:

Then there is a unique RR-algebra morphism u:S→Tu:S\to T, which lifts u¯\bar{u}, i.e. the following diagram also commutes:

This property is known under the name infinitesimal lifting. As we saw above, it reflects the definition of a local diffeomorphism inside of algebraic geometry. When dealing with a formally étale SS, we will often refer to the map ϕ:R→S\phi:R\to S as formally étale rather than to the RR-algebra itself.

To go from formally étale to étale ring maps, we need to recall the notion of finitely presented algebras. It is evident that an RR-algebra SS is always of the form S≅R[xi:i∈ℐ]/𝔞S\cong R[x_{i}:i\in\mathcal{I}]/\mathfrak{a} for some index set ℐ\mathcal{I} and an ideal 𝔞⊆R[xi:i∈ℐ]\mathfrak{a}\subseteq R[x_{i}:i\in\mathcal{I}]. In practice we are often interested in a finite number of generators and a finitely generated ideal, hence we define:

Definition.

Let RR be a ring. We say an RR-algebra SS is finitely presented if it is of the form S≅R⁡[x1,…,xn]/(f1,…,fm)S\cong R[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]/(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}) for some fi∈R⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{i}\in R[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m.

Naturally, we have immediately the following fact about transitivity: If SS if finitely presented over RR and TT is finitely presented over SS, then TT is finitely presented over RR. Note that a localization of RR at one element, say a∈Ra\in R, is finitely presented, since Ra≅R⁡[t]/(a​t−1)R_{a}\cong R[t]/(at-1). Therefore a localization at finitely many elements is still finitely presented, but this does not have to be true for any multiplicative system.

Definition.

Let SS be an RR-algebra. SS is called étale if it is formally étale and finitely presented.

The following lemma is a direct consequence of our definitions and observations.

Lemma 3.1.

Let SS be an RR-algebra and S′S^{\prime} an SS-algebra. Assume that R→SR\to S and S→S′S\to S^{\prime} are (formally) étale, then the induced map R→S′R\to S^{\prime} is also (formally) étale.

Another important fact which again follows easily from chasing the correct diagram states that the property of being étale is stable under base change. Before proving this statement, we want to recall the definition and add a simple remark: Let SS be an RR-algebra with ϕ:R→S\phi:R\to S the corresponding map and let R→R′R\to R^{\prime} be any ring homomorphism. Then the base change of ϕ\phi by R→R′R\to R^{\prime} is the ring map R′→R′⊗RS≕S′R^{\prime}\to R^{\prime}\otimes_{R}S\eqqcolon S^{\prime}.

Note that the explicit description of a base change is very natural when a presentation is given: We already saw that SS, being an RR-algebra, is of the form

S≅R[xi:i∈ℐ]/(fj:j∈𝒥),S\cong R[x_{i}:i\in\mathcal{I}]/(f_{j}:j\in\mathcal{J}),

for some index sets ℐ,𝒥\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J} and polynomials fj∈R[xi:i∈ℐ]f_{j}\in R[x_{i}:i\in\mathcal{I}]. Then, for the base change one has

R′⊗RS=R′[xi:i∈ℐ]/(fj′:j∈𝒥),R^{\prime}\otimes_{R}S=R^{\prime}[x_{i}:i\in\mathcal{I}]/(f_{j}^{\prime}:j\in\mathcal{J}),

where each fj′f_{j}^{\prime} is the image of fjf_{j} under the map R[xi:i∈ℐ]→R′[xi:i∈ℐ]R[x_{i}:i\in\mathcal{I}]\to R^{\prime}[x_{i}:i\in\mathcal{I}] induced by the map R→R′R\to R^{\prime}. In [Sta20, Tag 05G3] this fact is described as “the key to understanding base change”.

Lemma 3.2.

Let R→SR\to S be étale and R→R′R\to R^{\prime} be arbitrary. Then R′→R′⊗RSR^{\prime}\to R^{\prime}\otimes_{R}S is étale.

Corollary 3.3.

Let R→SR\to S and R→S′R\to S^{\prime} be étale. Then R→S⊗RS′R\to S\otimes_{R}S^{\prime} is étale.

The following proposition has a more involved proof.

Proposition 3.4.

Let RR be a ring, S=R​[x1,…,xn]g/(f1,…,fn)S=R[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]_{g}/(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}) for g∈R⁡[x1,…,xn]g\in R[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] and f1,…,fn∈R​[x1,…,xn]gf_{1},\dots,f_{n}\in R[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]_{g}. If the image of the Jacobian determinant det(∂fj∂xi)1≤i,j≤n\det(\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{i}})_{1\leq i,j\leq n} is invertible in SS, then SS is étale over RR.
Conversely, if R→SR\to S is étale, then there exists a presentation S=R⁡[x1,…,xn]/(f1,…,fn)S=R[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]/(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}) such that the image of det(∂fj∂xi)1≤i,j≤n\det(\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{i}})_{1\leq i,j\leq n} is invertible in SS.

For the proof we refer to standard literature [Ray70], [Mil80, Corollary 3.16], to well-written lecture notes [Mil13], [Hoc17] and to the Stacks Project [Sta20, Section 00U0].

Definition.

A finitely presented RR-algebra SS is called standard étale if it is of the form S=R​[t]g/(f)S=R[t]_{g}/(f) for some polynomials f,g∈R⁡[t]f,g\in R[t], such that ff is monic and its derivative f′f^{\prime} is invertible in SS.

Note that by Proposition 3.4, it follows that a standard étale algebra is indeed étale.

There exists a structure theorem of étale algebras, making sure that any étale algebra is locally standard étale. In [Gro67, p. 120] Grothendieck attributes this fact to Chevalley and so shall we.

Theorem 3.5 (Chevalley).

Let SS be a finitely presented RR-algebra. Then SS is étale over RR if and only if for every prime ideal 𝔮\mathfrak{q} of SS with contraction 𝔭\mathfrak{p} to RR there exist b∈S∖𝔮b\in S\setminus\mathfrak{q} and a∈R∖𝔭a\in R\setminus\mathfrak{p} such that SbS_{b} is isomorphic to a standard étale algebra over RaR_{a}.

The proof is an application of Zariski’s main theorem, a form of which we already mentioned in Lemma 2.5. Also Nakayama’s lemma and the primitive element theorem for separable field extensions play a role in the proof. In his lecture notes [Hoc17] Hochster points out that “additional trickery” is required as well. Therefore the proof is lengthy and technical and shall not be provided here. We refer to [Ray70, pp. 51], [Ive73, pp. 63] [Mil80, Theorem 3.14] as well as [Sta20, Tag 00UE], [Gro67, pp. 120] and [Hoc17, pp. 27].

3.3 Construction of the Henselization

We want to construct the Henselization of a local ring (R,𝔪,K)(R,\mathfrak{m},K) and consequently prove its existence and some desirable properties. First, we define the notion of étale neighborhoods like Milne in [Mil80]:

Definition.

Let (R,𝔪,K)(R,\mathfrak{m},K) be local. A pair (S,𝔮)(S,\mathfrak{q}) is called an étale neighborhood of RR if SS is an étale RR-algebra and 𝔮\mathfrak{q} is a prime of SS lying over 𝔪\mathfrak{m}, such that the induced map between the residue fields K=R/𝔪→S𝔮/𝔮​S𝔮K=R/\mathfrak{m}\to S_{\mathfrak{q}}/\mathfrak{q}S_{\mathfrak{q}} is an isomorphism.

In order to save notation in our setting, it is more useful to work locally and to use the notion of pointed étale extensions, as does Hochster in his lecture notes [Hoc17]:

Definition.

A local ring TT is called pointed étale extension of (R,𝔪,K)(R,\mathfrak{m},K) if T=S𝔮T=S_{\mathfrak{q}} for some étale neighborhood (S,𝔮)(S,\mathfrak{q}).

Before stating and proving a theorem which connects étale ring maps and Henselian rings, we need to state the following lemma.

Lemma 3.6.

Assume TT and T′T^{\prime} are pointed étale extensions of RR. Then there is at most one local RR-algebra homomorphism from TT to T′T^{\prime}.

The proof of this lemma requires the study the multiplication map, given by the linear extension of μ:S⊗RS↠S\mu:S\otimes_{R}S\twoheadrightarrow S sending s⊗s′↦s​s′s\otimes s^{\prime}\mapsto ss^{\prime}, and its kernel 𝔞≔ker⁡(μ)\mathfrak{a}\coloneqq\ker(\mu). We omit the details and refer to [Hoc17, pp. 45], [Ive73, p. 71], [Mil80, p. 36] and [Mil13, Section 4]. Now we are ready for the central theorem of this section. Its statement and proof can be found in the references just mentioned, however we shall reprove it again following the notes of Hochster.

Theorem 3.7.

Let (R,𝔪,K)(R,\mathfrak{m},K) a be local ring. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    RR is Henselian.

  2. (2)

    If f∈R⁡[t]f\in R[t] is a monic polynomial whose reduction mod 𝔪\mathfrak{m}, f¯∈K⁡[t]\bar{f}\in K[t], has a simple root λ∈K\lambda\in K, then there exists an element r∈Rr\in R such that r≡λmod𝔪r\equiv\lambda\mod\mathfrak{m} and f⁡(r)=0f(r)=0.

  3. (3)

    If R→TR\to T is a pointed étale extension, then R≅TR\cong T.

    If f1,…,fn∈R⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\dots,f_{n}\in R[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] are nn polynomials in nn variables whose images fj¯mod𝔪\overline{f_{j}}\mod\mathfrak{m} vanish simultaneously at (λ1,…,λn)∈Kn(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n})\in K^{n} and the Jacobian determinant det(∂fj∂xi)\det(\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}) does not vanishmod𝔪\mod\mathfrak{m} at x1=λ1,…,xn=λnx_{1}=\lambda_{1},\dots,x_{n}=\lambda_{n}, then there are unique elements r1,…,rn∈Rr_{1},\dots,r_{n}\in R such that for all ii, we have ri≡λimod𝔪r_{i}\equiv\lambda_{i}\mod\mathfrak{m} and fj​(r1,…,rn)=0,1≤j≤nf_{j}(r_{1},\dots,r_{n})=0,1\leq j\leq n.

This theorem gives a deep insight into Henselian rings. In particular, the equivalence of conditions (1)(1) and (2)(2) implies that it suffices to lift only simple roots in order to be able to lift coprime factorizations. Applying this for the ring of algebraic power series and Theorem 1.7 we obtain a proof for Theorem 1.8. We see that Henselian rings are connected to the theory of étale ring maps via condition (3)(3). Moreover, (4)(4) is a multidimensional version of Hensel’s lemma for nn polynomials and nn variables; if the fif_{i}’s were also allowed to be power series, one would recognize the implicit function theorem. The equivalence (1)⇔(4)(1)\Leftrightarrow(4) states that a ring is Henselian if and only if the algebraic version of this analytic theorem holds in this ring.

Proof.

We will show that (1)⇒(2)⇒(3)⇒(4)⇒(1)(1)\Rightarrow(2)\Rightarrow(3)\Rightarrow(4)\Rightarrow(1).

(1)⇒(2)(1)\Rightarrow(2): Suppose RR is Henselian and we have a monic f∈R⁡[t]f\in R[t] such that f¯\bar{f} has a simple root λ∈K\lambda\in K. The polynomials t−λt-\lambda and g¯​(t)\bar{g}(t) are relatively prime. Using the assumption we find a lifting of the factorization to f⁡(t)=(t−r)​g​(t)f(t)=(t-r)g(t) for some r≡λmod𝔪r\equiv\lambda\mod\mathfrak{m} and g∈R⁡[t]g\in R[t]. Clearly f⁡(r)=0f(r)=0.

However, since ϕ\phi and RR are local, we have that T≅Rϕ−1​(𝔮)≅RT\cong R_{\phi^{-1}(\mathfrak{q})}\cong R, what was to be shown.

Having in mind that (1)⇔(3)(1)\Leftrightarrow(3) in this theorem, we come back to our goal of constructing the Henselization. We see that it may be a good idea to combine all possible pointed étale extensions of RR into one large ring. If we can do this rigorously, then we might argue that this ring does not have any proper pointed étale extensions anymore, which will mean that it will be Henselian. Finally, we might be able to verify the universal property of the Henselization and conclude that we indeed found the correct object. Let us start executing this plan.

Given a local ring RR, we wish to define a set of pointed étale algebras of RR, say ℛ\mathcal{R}, that contains exactly one representative from each isomorphism class of pointed étale extensions. It is not trivial that ℛ\mathcal{R} is a set, since it might turn out “too large”. However, the following result bounds the cardinality of a pointed étale extension from above and allows us to define ℛ\mathcal{R} properly.

Lemma 3.8.

Let RR be a local ring and TT a pointed étale extension. Then TT is finite if RR is finite. In the other case, the cardinalities of RR and TT agree.

Proof.

By definition, T=S𝔮T=S_{\mathfrak{q}} for some prime 𝔮⊆S\mathfrak{q}\subseteq S and an étale RR-algebra SS. Since SS is finitely presented over RR, we have |S|≤|R|n|S|\leq|R|^{n} for some n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, where |⋅||\cdot| denotes cardinality. The localization is parametrized by pairs in (S∖𝔮)×S(S\setminus\mathfrak{q})\times S and therefore |S𝔮|≤|S|2|S_{\mathfrak{q}}|\leq|S|^{2}. We have

|R|≤|T|=|S𝔮|≤|R|2​n,|R|\leq|T|=|S_{\mathfrak{q}}|\leq|R|^{2n},

proving the assertion. ∎

Now, from the axiom of choice, it follows that the set ℛ\mathcal{R} exists, since it is a subset of the set of all ring structures on a set with similar cardinality as RR. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an index set of ℛ\mathcal{R}, whereby index set means that each i∈𝒜i\in\mathcal{A} corresponds bijectively to a Ti∈ℛT_{i}\in\mathcal{R} and we can write therefore ℛ=(Ti)i∈𝒜.\mathcal{R}=(T_{i})_{i\in\mathcal{A}}.

Proposition 3.9.

For i,j∈𝒜i,j\in\mathcal{A} define i≤ji\leq j if and only if there exists a local RR-algebra map ϕi,j:Ti→Tj\phi_{i,j}:T_{i}\to T_{j}. Then (𝒜,≤)(\mathcal{A},\leq) is a directed set.

Proof.

Obviously, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is not empty since ℛ\mathcal{R} contains RR. Clearly, ≤\leq is reflexive, as one always has the identity map id:Ti→Ti\text{id}:T_{i}\to T_{i} for all ii. Moreover, if we have ϕ:Ti→Tj\phi:T_{i}\to T_{j} and ψ:Tj→Tk\psi:T_{j}\to T_{k} both local RR-algebra maps then ψ∘ϕ:Ti→Tk\psi\circ\phi:T_{i}\to T_{k} is a local RR-algebra map. This implies that ≤\leq is transitive. Finally, we have to prove that for any two Ti,Tj∈ℛT_{i},T_{j}\in\mathcal{R}, there exist Tk∈ℛT_{k}\in\mathcal{R} and two local RR-algebra maps Ti→TkT_{i}\to T_{k} and Tj→TkT_{j}\to T_{k}. As Ti,TjT_{i},T_{j} are pointed étale, they are localizations of some étale RR-algebras Si,SjS_{i},S_{j}. By Corollary 3.3 we immediately have that R→Si⊗RSjR\to S_{i}\otimes_{R}S_{j} is étale. Consider the composite map

R→Si⊗RSj↠K⊗KK→≅K,R\to S_{i}\otimes_{R}S_{j}\twoheadrightarrow K\otimes_{K}K\xrightarrow{\cong}K,

which sends r↦r⋅(1Si⊗1Sj)↦r¯⋅(1K⊗1K)↦r¯r\mapsto r\cdot(1_{S_{i}}\otimes 1_{S_{j}})\mapsto\bar{r}\cdot(1_{K}\otimes 1_{K})\mapsto\bar{r} and is thus precisely the quotient map R↠R/𝔪≅KR\twoheadrightarrow R/\mathfrak{m}\cong K. It follows that by letting QQ be the kernel of the map Si⊗RSj↠K⊗KKS_{i}\otimes_{R}S_{j}\twoheadrightarrow K\otimes_{K}K, we must have that R→(Si⊗RSj)QR\to(S_{i}\otimes_{R}S_{j})_{Q} is local. The residue class field of (Si⊗RSj)Q(S_{i}\otimes_{R}S_{j})_{Q} is KK. Set Tk=(Si⊗RSj)QT_{k}=(S_{i}\otimes_{R}S_{j})_{Q} which is now by definition a pointed étale extension of RR and we have maps Ti→TkT_{i}\to T_{k} and Tj→TkT_{j}\to T_{k}. This shows the existence of a k∈𝒜k\in\mathcal{A} for given i,j∈𝒜i,j\in\mathcal{A} such that i,j≤ki,j\leq k and finishes the proof. ∎

This proposition shows that (ℛ,{ϕi,j:Ti→Tj}i,j∈𝒜,i≤j)(\mathcal{R},\{\phi_{i,j}:T_{i}\to T_{j}\}_{i,j\in\mathcal{A},i\leq j}) forms a direct system of rings. Note that because of Lemma 3.6, we know that the ϕi,j\phi_{i,j}’s are actually unique, justifying that the construction is canonical. The fact that ℛ\mathcal{R} together with these maps forms a direct system of rings allows us to define the direct limit:

Definition.

For a local ring (R,𝔪,K)(R,\mathfrak{m},K) we denote Re≔lim→T∈ℛ⁡TR^{\text{e}}\coloneqq\varinjlim_{T\in\mathcal{R}}T.

Given a local ring RR, we combine all pointed étale extensions of it to the ring ReR^{\text{e}} in a rigorous way using the direct limit in the definition above. Therefore, it is natural to expect that ReR^{\text{e}} does not have any proper pointed étale extensions anymore, which means that ReR^{\text{e}} is Henselian by Theorem 3.7. It is also intuitively clear that ReR^{\text{e}} the “smallest” extension of RR that admits this property. We prove both statements below using ideas from [Ive73] and [Hoc17].

Lemma 3.10.

Let (R,𝔪,K)(R,\mathfrak{m},K) be a local ring. Then ReR^{\text{e}} is local with maximal ideal 𝔪​R\mathfrak{m}R and residue field KK. Moreover, ReR^{\text{e}} is Henselian.

Proof.

Locality, the statement about the maximal ideal and the condition on the residue field follow by construction, since every pointed étale RR-algebra TT is local with maximal ideal 𝔪​T\mathfrak{m}T and residue field KK.

By Theorem 3.7 we only have to check the lifting of simple roots in order to verify the Henselian property. Let f∈Re​[t]f\in R^{\text{e}}[t] be monic and λ∈K\lambda\in K a simple root of f¯∈K⁡[t]\bar{f}\in K[t]. Since Re=lim→T∈ℛ⁡TR^{\text{e}}=\varinjlim_{T\in\mathcal{R}}T, there exists some pointed étale RR-algebra TT such that all coefficients of ff lie in TT. We define T′≔(T⁡[t]/(f))𝔮T^{\prime}\coloneqq(T[t]/(f))_{\mathfrak{q}}, where 𝔮≔(t¯−λ)\mathfrak{q}\coloneqq(\bar{t}-\lambda). The residue field of T′T^{\prime} is KK and because λ\lambda is a simple root, it follows that f′f^{\prime} is invertible in T′T^{\prime} and therefore T′T^{\prime} is a pointed étale extension of RR by Lemma 3.1 and Proposition 3.4. However, ff has a root in T′T^{\prime} and it lifts λ\lambda. This gives rise to an element r∈Rer\in R^{\text{e}} such that f⁡(r)=0f(r)=0 and r¯=λ\bar{r}=\lambda. ∎

Theorem 3.11.

Let (R,𝔪,K)(R,\mathfrak{m},K) be a local ring. The Henselization of RR is given by the direct limit as in Definition Definition: Rh=ReR^{\text{h}}=R^{\text{e}}.

Proof.

We will verify the universal property. From the lemma above we already have that ReR^{\text{e}} is local and Henselian. Let ψ:R→H\psi:R\to H be a local map from RR to a Henselian ring (H,𝔪H,L)(H,\mathfrak{m}_{H},L). To show that this map factors uniquely through ReR^{\text{e}}, it suffices to show that it factors uniquely through every (T,𝔮​T,K)(T,\mathfrak{q}T,K), where T=S𝔮T=S_{\mathfrak{q}} is a pointed étale extension of RR. Consider the commutative diagram of the base change:

Since R→SR\to S is étale, we obtain by Lemma 3.2 that H→S⊗RHH\to S\otimes_{R}H is also étale. Moreover, there exists a canonical map S⊗RH→K⊗KL≅LS\otimes_{R}H\to K\otimes_{K}L\cong L. Denote its kernel by QQ. It follows that H→(S⊗RH)QH\to(S\otimes_{R}H)_{Q} is a localization of an étale extension. Since L≅K⊗KLL\cong K\otimes_{K}L, we obtain that the residue fields agree and hence this extension is pointed étale. But HH is Henselian, hence H≅(S⊗RH)QH\cong(S\otimes_{R}H)_{Q} by (1)⇒(3)(1)\Rightarrow(3) of Theorem 3.7 and therefore we found a local map ϕ:S→(S⊗RH)Q≅H\phi:S\to(S\otimes_{R}H)_{Q}\cong H, the map we were looking for:

Finally, because HH is pointed étale over itself as well as over (S⊗RH)Q(S\otimes_{R}H)_{Q}, we obtain that this map is unique by Lemma 3.6. ∎

The characterization of the Henselization as a direct limit of pointed étale extensions not only proves its existence, but also led to remarkable mathematical discoveries in this area in the second half of the last century. The theory of approximation rings and consequently the algebraic version of Artin’s Approximation [Art69] use exactly this fact (amongst other). This and other related results are contained in the recent survey [Hau17] by Hauser. The Henselization of non-local rings with respect to ideals is investigated in [Gre69]. An exposition of various versions of the Henselian property can be found in [Rib85]. The connection of Henselian rings to rings satisfying Weierstrass preparation theorem was first established by Lafon in 1967 [Laf67]. Probably the most explicit application of the Theorems 3.5 and 3.11 was found by Denef and Lipshitz in 1985 and we shall explain their ideas in the next section.

4 Explicit Implications

4.1 Proof of Theorem 1.1

It is easy to verify that the derivative of the minimal polynomial P⁡(x,t)P(x,t) of hh does not vanish at the origin, ∂tP⁡(0,0)=∂tP~​(0,h~​(0))≠0\partial_{t}P(0,0)=\partial_{t}\tilde{P}(0,\tilde{h}(0))\neq 0, and that we have again

f=a0+a1​h+⋯+ar​hrb0+b1​h+⋯+bs​hs,f=\frac{a_{0}+a_{1}h+\dots+a_{r}h^{r}}{b_{0}+b_{1}h+\dots+b_{s}h^{s}},

for polynomials ai,bj∈K⁡[x]a_{i},b_{j}\in K[x] such that b0​(0)=b~​(0,h~​(0))≠0b_{0}(0)=\tilde{b}(0,\tilde{h}(0))\neq 0. ∎

Now we can finally prove Theorem 1.1.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Using the theorem above it follows that there exist r,s∈ℕr,s\in\mathbb{N} and ai​(x),bj​(x)∈K⁡[x]a_{i}(x),b_{j}(x)\in K[x] for 0≤i≤r0\leq i\leq r, 0≤j≤s0\leq j\leq s with b0​(0)≠0b_{0}(0)\neq 0 such that

f⁡(x)=a0​(x)+a1​(x)​h​(x)+⋯+ar​(x)​h​(x)rb0​(x)+b1​(x)​h​(x)+⋯+bs​(x)​h​(x)s,\displaystyle f(x)=\frac{a_{0}(x)+a_{1}(x)h(x)+\dots+a_{r}(x)h(x)^{r}}{b_{0}(x)+b_{1}(x)h(x)+\dots+b_{s}(x)h(x)^{s}}, (6)

where h⁡(x)∈K​⟨x⟩h(x)\in K\langle x\rangle is étale-algebraic. Define

W⁡(x,t)≔a0​(x)+a1​(x)​t+⋯+ar​(x)​trb0​(x)+b1​(x)​t+⋯+bs​(x)​ts∈K​[x,t](x,t),\displaystyle W(x,t)\coloneqq\frac{a_{0}(x)+a_{1}(x)t+\dots+a_{r}(x)t^{r}}{b_{0}(x)+b_{1}(x)t+\dots+b_{s}(x)t^{s}}\in K[x,t]_{(x,t)},

and let

R⁡(x,t)≔W⁡(x​t,t)​t​∂tP⁡(x​t,t)P⁡(x​t,t).\displaystyle R(x,t)\coloneqq W(xt,t)t\frac{\partial_{t}P(xt,t)}{P(xt,t)}.

Using Lemma 1.2 and the same computation as in equation (3) we verify that we found the correct rational function:

𝒟⁡(R⁡(x,t))=W⁡(x,h⁡(x))=h⁡(x).∎\mathcal{D}(R(x,t))=W(x,h(x))=h(x).\qed

4.2 Codes of Algebraic Power Series

Finally, we introduce a new result which can be seen as a corollary of Theorem 4.1. First, we remark that the following fact was explained in [AM65, pp. 88] and became later known under the name Artin-Mazur lemma, see [BCR98, AMR92]. In [Ron18, Proposition 9.3] a more general version of the statement, allowing for KK to be any complete normal local domain (with appropriate changes to the assumptions), is presented.

Theorem 4.2 (Artin & Mazur).

Let f∈K⁡⟨x1,…,xn⟩=K⁡⟨x⟩f\in K\langle x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\rangle=K\langle x\rangle be an algebraic power series with f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0. Then there exist k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and a vector of kk polynomials P⁡(x,y1,…,yk)∈K⁡[x]​[y1,…,yk]kP(x,y_{1},\dots,y_{k})\in K[x][y_{1},\dots,y_{k}]^{k} with the following properties:

  1. (1)

    P⁡(x,f,h2,…,hk)=0P(x,f,h_{2},\dots,h_{k})=0 for algebraic power series h2,…,hk∈K⁡⟨x⟩h_{2},\dots,h_{k}\in K\langle x\rangle with hi​(0)=0h_{i}(0)=0 for i=2,…,ki=2,\dots,k.

  2. (2)

    The Jacobian matrix JP​(x,y1,…,yk)J_{P}(x,y_{1},\dots,y_{k}) of P⁡(x,y1,…,yn)P(x,y_{1},\dots,y_{n}) with respect to the variables y1,…,yky_{1},\dots,y_{k} at x=y=0x=y=0 is invertible: JP​(0,0)∈GLk⁡(K)J_{P}(0,0)\in\GL_{k}(K).

In other words, given f∈K​⟨x⟩f\in K\langle x\rangle, one can find k−1k-1 algebraic power series h2,…,hk∈K⁡⟨x⟩h_{2},\dots,h_{k}\in K\langle x\rangle and a kk-dimensional vector of polynomials P⁡(x,y1,…,yk)∈K​[x,y]kP(x,y_{1},\dots,y_{k})\in K[x,y]^{k}, such that P⁡(x,f⁡(x),h2​(x),…,hk​(x))=0P(x,f(x),h_{2}(x),\dots,h_{k}(x))=0 and the Jacobian of P⁡(x,y)P(x,y) with respect to yy at x=y=0x=y=0 is invertible. Similarly to Theorem 4.1, this implies that one can repair the problem of an algebraic power series of not being étale-algebraic, now by appending k−1k-1 new power series and considering the kk-dimensional analogue of the definition of étale-algebraicity. This polynomial vector P⁡(x,y)∈K​[x,y]kP(x,y)\in K[x,y]^{k} is referred to as a (mother) code of the algebraic series ff in [ACJH18, Hau17, AMR92]. The authors Alonso, Castro-Jimenez and Hauser of the first reference point out that “The advantage of this code in comparison with taking the minimal polynomial lies in the fact that the latter determines the algebraic series only up to conjugation, so that extra information is necessary to specify the series, typically a sufficiently high truncation of the Taylor expansion. In contrast, the polynomial code determines the series completely and is easy to handle algebraically”.

With the help of the theorem of Denef and Lipshitz we can improve on the Artin-Mazur lemma, proving that it is always possible to choose k=2k=2. Note that since Theorem 1.1 is known to hold in more generality, it is also natural that also the general version by Rond can be covered and improved by our approach.

Theorem 4.3.

Let f∈K⁡⟨x1,…,xn⟩=K⁡⟨x⟩f\in K\langle x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\rangle=K\langle x\rangle be an algebraic power series with f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0. Then there exists a vector of two polynomials P⁡(x,y1,y2)∈K⁡[x]​[y1,y2]2P(x,y_{1},y_{2})\in K[x][y_{1},y_{2}]^{2} with the following properties:

  1. (1)

    P⁡(x,f,h)=0P(x,f,h)=0 for some étale-algebraic power series h∈K​⟨x⟩h\in K\langle x\rangle.

  2. (2)

    The Jacobian matrix JP​(x,y1,y2)J_{P}(x,y_{1},y_{2}) of P⁡(x,y1,y2)P(x,y_{1},y_{2}) with respect to y1y_{1} and y2y_{2} at 00 is invertible: JP​(0,0,0)∈GL2⁡(K)J_{P}(0,0,0)\in\GL_{2}(K).

Note that in the two-dimensional square matrix JP​(0,0,0)J_{P}(0,0,0), the first 00 means setting the variables x1,…,xnx_{1},\dots,x_{n} all to 00 in JP​(x,y1,y2)J_{P}(x,y_{1},y_{2}), whereas the other two zeros are both one-dimensional and advert to y1y_{1} and y2y_{2}.

Proof.

Let Q⁡(x,y1)Q(x,y_{1}) be the minimal polynomial of ff. If ∂y1Q⁡(0,0)≠0\partial_{y_{1}}Q(0,0)\neq 0 then we can simply choose P⁡(x,y1,y2)=(Q⁡(x,y1),y2)P(x,y_{1},y_{2})=(Q(x,y_{1}),y_{2}) and the assertion follows in this case.

We are left with the more challenging case ∂y1Q⁡(0,0)=0\partial_{y_{1}}Q(0,0)=0. By Theorem 4.1, we may write for some étale-algebraic power series h∈K​⟨x⟩h\in K\langle x\rangle

f=a0+a1​h+⋯+ar​hrb0+b1​h+⋯+bs​hs,\displaystyle f=\frac{a_{0}+a_{1}h+\dots+a_{r}h^{r}}{b_{0}+b_{1}h+\dots+b_{s}h^{s}}, (7)

for r,s∈ℕr,s\in\mathbb{N} and ai​(x),bj​(x)∈K⁡[x]a_{i}(x),b_{j}(x)\in K[x] with 0≤i≤r0\leq i\leq r, 0≤j≤s0\leq j\leq s and b0​(0)≠0b_{0}(0)\neq 0. Define the polynomials

T1​(x,y2)\displaystyle T_{1}(x,y_{2}) ≔a0​(x)+a1​(x)​y2+⋯+ar​(x)​y2r,\displaystyle\coloneqq a_{0}(x)+a_{1}(x)y_{2}+\dots+a_{r}(x)y_{2}^{r},
T2​(x,y2)\displaystyle T_{2}(x,y_{2}) ≔b0​(x)+b1​(x)​y2+⋯+bs​(x)​y2s,\displaystyle\coloneqq b_{0}(x)+b_{1}(x)y_{2}+\dots+b_{s}(x)y_{2}^{s},

and get the relationship T1​(x,h⁡(x))=f⁡(x)​T2​(x,h⁡(x))T_{1}(x,h(x))=f(x)T_{2}(x,h(x)) from identity (7). Let S⁡(x,y2)S(x,y_{2}) be the minimal polynomial of the étale-algebraic h⁡(x)h(x), so that ∂y2S⁡(0,0)≠0\partial_{y_{2}}S(0,0)\neq 0. Now we put

P⁡(x,y1,y2)≔(y1​T2​(x,y2)−T1​(x,y2)S⁡(x,y2)).\displaystyle P(x,y_{1},y_{2})\coloneqq\begin{pmatrix}y_{1}T_{2}(x,y_{2})-T_{1}(x,y_{2})\\ S(x,y_{2})\end{pmatrix}.

A simple computation confirms that this choice of PP satisfies all required properties:

P⁡(x,f⁡(x),h⁡(x))\displaystyle P(x,f(x),h(x)) =0and\displaystyle=0\hskip 14.22636pt\text{and}
JP​(0,0,0)=(T2​(x,y2)∗0∂y2S⁡(x,y2))\displaystyle J_{P}(0,0,0)=\begin{pmatrix}T_{2}(x,y_{2})&*\\ 0&\partial_{y_{2}}S(x,y_{2})\end{pmatrix} |(0,0,0)=(T2​(0,0)∗0∂y2S⁡(0,0)).\displaystyle\Bigg|_{(0,0,0)}=\begin{pmatrix}T_{2}(0,0)&*\\ 0&\partial_{y_{2}}S(0,0)\end{pmatrix}.

Clearly, det(JP​(0,0,0))=T2​(0,0)​∂y2S⁡(0,0)≠0\det(J_{P}(0,0,0))=T_{2}(0,0)\partial_{y_{2}}S(0,0)\neq 0, because both factors are different from 00. ∎
